title: Nora and the Sleepy Rain
markdown:
Nora the lamb was nestled deep in her soft straw bed inside the sheep’s cozy house, a place that usually felt like the warmest hug in the world. The woolly blankets, spun from the finest light fluff, were pulled right up to her chin. Outside her little window, moonlight spilled silver trails on the meadow floor. Yet Nora’s eyes were wide open. Sleep, it seemed, had decided to take a very long holiday.

The world outside, under the bright eye of the sun, was usually Nora’s favourite place. She loved the sweet smell of clover that tickled her nose and the way the tall grass tickled her woolly tummy when she played. But when the sun went to sleep behind the gentle hills, and the big friendly moon took its place in the velvety sky, the quiet of the meadow sometimes felt a little too quiet. It was a stillness that made Nora’s little lamby brain hum with thoughts, unable to switch off and drift into dreamland.

One lovely night, as Nora watched the moonbeams play peek-a-boo with the leaves of the old oak tree, a small shimmering shape zipped past her nose, quick as a wink. It was a moth, wings like delicate dusted silver, dancing a silent ballet in the gentle moonlight.

“Oh,” whispered Nora, a tiny hopeful thought beginning to bloom like a little daisy. “Perhaps if I count them, I can feel sleepy, just like Mama says.”

She watched another moth dance by, then another, and another. They were so quick and graceful, like little waltzing stars that had come down to play. “One… two… oh, where did that one go? Was it three? No, maybe four?” Nora giggled softly, a tiny rustle in the quiet air. It was far too hard to keep track of their speedy little dances. The moths were just too speedy, and her counting got all muddled, like a ball of yarn playfully unravelled by a kitten.

Just then, a gentle voice, as soft as a whisper of wings, floated from the moonlit meadow. “Hello there, little lamb,” it said, warm and kind. Nora peeked out from under her blanket. It was Flicker, a moth with wings like moonlight spun into the finest most delicate lace. He hovered nearby, long slender antennae wiggling kindly. “You seem to have many awake thoughts for this sleepy time of night,” Flicker observed, his voice a gentle comforting hum, like the distant buzz of bees on a warm afternoon.

Nora told Flicker all about her wide-awake problem and her bright idea of counting the moths. Flicker chuckled, a sound like tiny tinkling bells that did not disturb the quiet at all. “Ah, little lamb,” he hummed, “moths are a bit like shy secrets. They don’t always like to be counted directly; they prefer to dance their own gentle dances. But we can try counting other things together. Perhaps the sleepy dandelions that are nodding their heads, dreaming of tomorrow’s sunshine?”

So Nora and Flicker began a quiet counting adventure. First they looked at the lovely silver trails the moon made on the dewy grass. “That’s very pretty,” Nora said, “but it doesn’t make me feel sleepy.” Then they gently turned their attention to the fuzzy little seed heads of the dandelions, all tucked in for the night, tiny parachutes ready for the morning breeze. “One, two, three…” Nora began, but a gentle breeze rustled the flowers, and the seed heads wiggled and swayed. Nora’s eyes felt a little less wide, but sleep was still being very shy.

Flicker then suggested, with a flutter of his wings, that they count the silver moths again, only this time extra quiet and patient, like little woodland detectives. Nora tried her very best. She watched them swirl and twirl in the moonlight, like tiny silken dancers. She counted and counted, her voice a soft murmur, “Seventeen… eighteen… nineteen…” but still her eyes felt wide and bright, like two little lamps. The moths, one by one, began to flutter into the velvety petals of the night-blooming flowers and under the sheltering leaves, seeking their own cozy spots for rest.

Flicker landed gently on a soft blade of grass beside Nora’s warm wool. “The moths are all asleep now, little one,” he whispered. Nora sighed, a tiny disappointed sound. The meadow was quiet again, and the wide-awake feeling seemed to be growing bigger, like a little cloud expanding in her mind. She wished with all her might that she could just close her eyes and float away to the land of sweet dreams.

Just as a little worry, like a tiny ticklish spider, started to creep around Nora’s woolly ears, a new sound began to whisper across the meadow. It was not loud. It was a soft steady pitter-patter, like tiny raindrops tapping a gentle rhythm on the leaves above. The air grew cool and smelled so fresh. Nora tilted her head, ears twitching. What was that gentle rhythmic drumming?

Flicker’s antennae wiggled with quiet delight. “That,” he hummed, “is the rain, beginning its soft lullaby on the meadow roof. It’s singing the world to sleep.”

Nora listened very closely. Pitter-patter… pitter-patter… It was a slow gentle rhythm, like a tiny soft heartbeat echoing the rhythm of her own slowing breath. It was not like the quick zipping moths or the wobbly dandelions. This sound was steady, calm, and wonderfully comforting. Nora started to count, softly at first. “Pitter… patter… pitter… patter…” And then, as she continued to count the soft lovely sounds, a wonderful thing happened. Her eyelids began to feel heavy, like little velvet curtains slowly drawing shut. The pitter-patter was like a special song, a lullaby sung just for her, by the gentle rain.

With Flicker humming a soft gentle tune nearby, a sound like the rustle of silk, Nora let the rain count her to sleep. Pitter-patter… pitter-patter… Her breath grew slower, deeper, each breath a gentle wave of sleepiness. The silver moonlight did not seem so bright anymore; it softened and blurred at the edges. She snuggled down, feeling safe and warm, the gentle drumming of the rain a perfect peaceful rhythm that smoothed away all her awake thoughts. Soon Nora the lamb drifted into sweet quiet dreams, the meadow wrapped in a soft rainy lullaby, Flicker a gentle guardian nearby.
